rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. An intermediate temperature leaves room to explore selectivity in either direction.
Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to probe selectivity of the single critical pair at R = 0.62. The current elution window leaves ample room to adjust gradient slope later if needed.

Test the upper temperature limit to determine whether the central critical pair becomes fully resolved. Monitor the neighboring central peaks as well, since their spacing decreased at 50 C and may become limiting.

Use an intermediate temperature to balance the two competing central separations, and a shallower gradient to improve resolution. The last peak should still have a reasonable margin below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

The maximum CRF is secured at injection 4; shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This tests whether the critical central pair retains R ≥ 1.5 under modest compression.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover the marginal R = 1.47 separation while preserving the other critical pair. This should interpolate between injections 4 and 5, potentially retaining CRF 1.000 with earlier final elution than injection 4.

Raise both gradient endpoints by 0.05, preserving the successful slope from injection 6 while seeking earlier elution. This tests whether a stronger starting solvent maintains the two critical central separations.

Probe lower-temperature selectivity as an alternative route to a faster fully resolved method. The critical central peaks appear to change order between 40 and 50 C, so moving below that crossover may open their separation while keeping final elution below 10 minutes.

Test a weaker starting solvent with a steeper gradient at the successful 55 C temperature. Lowering phi0 may restore the limiting central separation while the steeper slope keeps final elution earlier than the fully resolved 8.00-minute result.

Reduce the slope from injection 9 to improve the R = 1.17 central separation while checking that the neighboring R = 1.54 pair remains resolved. This could recover CRF 1.000 with final elution earlier than 8 minutes.

With CRF 1.000 secured, test a faster, stronger-starting gradient at 60 C for an alternative selectivity window beyond the central-pair crossover. Check both the central cluster and early peaks for resolution loss.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover early-peak spacing, while steepening the gradient to probe separation beyond the central crossover at 60 C. This tests a faster alternative without sacrificing the already secured maximum-score methods.

Probe an intermediate low-temperature selectivity window with a shorter gradient. The 30 and 40 C runs show substantial rearrangement of the central cluster, so 35 C may balance those separations while keeping final elution comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether a stronger starting solvent at 50 C opens the critical central pair while retaining sufficient early-peak spacing. This explores a potentially faster alternative to the fully resolved 55 C methods.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 40 C separates the central pair on the opposite side of its temperature-driven crossover. The stronger starting solvent should offset some added retention, targeting full resolution within 10 minutes.

Combine a stronger start with a shallower gradient at 35 C to spread the crowded central cluster seen in injection 13. This tests another selectivity window while aiming to offset the slower gradient with earlier overall elution.

Test the lower temperature limit for an alternative elution order that may separate the central cluster beyond the crossover seen at 30–35 C. A stronger start and short gradient target earlier final elution than the current fastest fully resolved method.

Refine the successful 55 C region with a slope between injections 5 and 6, targeting full resolution with final elution below 8 minutes. This may provide a better critical-pair margin than the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10.

Increase the final organic fraction by one grid step from the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10, to test its speed boundary. The main risk is loss of the central R = 1.59 separation; retain injection 10 if it falls below 1.5.

Back off the gradient slope from injection 7 to recover its limiting central separation while retaining the stronger starting solvent. This tests whether that starting composition offers a useful fully resolved alternative before further shortening.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 10’s successful slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. All peaks should elute before the gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, preserving full resolution with a lower final organic fraction.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 21 to test the speed boundary of the shorter gradient. This slope lies between the fully resolved injection 10 and injection 9, so the central separation will determine whether any time saving is acceptable.

Back off the slope near the fastest fully resolved method to characterize its resolution margin. This should improve the earlier central separation, while testing whether the neighboring pair remains above R = 1.5 as the gradient becomes shallower.

Further flatten injection 20’s gradient to bring its limiting central pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the neighboring pair’s larger margin. This targets a more robust maximum-score alternative, with final elution expected below 10 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 24’s successful slope to seek earlier final elution while retaining its larger critical-pair margins. The maximum CRF is already secured; injections 10 and 21 remain the fastest fully resolved methods observed.
